ANTITRUST RISK ASSESSMENT AND HSR FILING STRATEGY MEMORANDUM

TO:      Deal Team / Client Counsel
FROM:    Antitrust & Competition Practice
DATE:    [Engagement Date]
RE:      Industrial Gas Distribution Acquisition — Antitrust Risk Assessment and HSR Filing Strategy (PE Buyer; Horizontal Overlap)
FILE:    antitrust-risk-memo.docx
STATUS:  Confidential — Attorney Work Product

================================================================================
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
================================================================================

This memorandum assesses antitrust risk and recommends an HSR Act filing and clearance strategy for the proposed private equity acquisition of an industrial gas distribution business involving horizontal overlap with an existing portfolio company or controlled affiliate in the same or adjacent product and geographic markets.

Primary conclusions:

1. The transaction is expected to be HSR-reportable if the size-of-transaction and size-of-person thresholds are met (or the size-of-person test is inapplicable). Filing should be planned on the early termination / standard 30-day initial waiting period track, with readiness for a Second Request if overlap markets draw agency interest.

2. Horizontal overlap in industrial gas distribution (packaged/cylinder gases, bulk liquid gases, and related delivery and services) is the principal substantive risk. Industrial gases are often analyzed on a product-by-product and local/regional geographic basis because of transportation costs, cylinder logistics, and customer switching patterns.

3. Risk level is preliminarily MODERATE, subject to confirmation of: (a) overlapping SKUs and service lines; (b) local share and concentration (HHI) in each overlap geography; (c) customer concentration and bid history; (d) franchise, supply, and non-compete arrangements; and (e) any prior agency scrutiny of the buyer’s platform or the target.

4. Recommended strategy: (i) complete a rapid overlap screen and share model before signing if not already done; (ii) negotiate robust antitrust efforts, timing, and reverse-termination / ticking-fee mechanics in the purchase agreement; (iii) prepare a clean, advocacy-oriented HSR filing with voluntary second-request readiness materials; (iv) consider early engagement with FTC/DOJ only if the overlap screen shows high concentration or prior agency attention; and (v) identify workable divestiture or behavioral remedies in advance for any local markets that are not defensible.

================================================================================
II. TRANSACTION OVERVIEW (FROM DEAL MATERIALS)
================================================================================

A. Structure and Parties

- Transaction type: Private equity acquisition of an industrial gas distribution business (asset or equity purchase, as reflected in the operative agreement).
- Competitive dimension: PE acquisition with horizontal overlap — the buyer’s existing portfolio includes one or more industrial gas distribution or adjacent businesses that compete with the target in overlapping product lines and/or territories.
- Operative agreement: Contains customary representations and warranties, covenants (including antitrust cooperation and efforts), conditions to closing (including HSR clearance), indemnification, and termination provisions. Open issues include deviations from firm precedent in the counterparty’s latest markup, which should be aligned with the filing and remedy strategy below.

B. Industry Context — Industrial Gas Distribution

Industrial gas distribution typically involves:

- Product segments: atmospheric gases (oxygen, nitrogen, argon), CO₂, hydrogen, acetylene, specialty and medical gases, dry ice, and related equipment/services (cylinder rental, bulk tank installation, telemetry, on-site generation support).
- Channels: packaged/cylinder, microbulk, bulk liquid, and pipeline or on-site in limited cases.
- Geography: Often local or regional for packaged gases and many bulk routes due to haul distance, depot density, and service response times; some specialty gases and national account programs are broader.
- Customers: Fabrication and manufacturing, healthcare, food and beverage, laboratories, construction, and energy/chemicals.
- Competitive dynamics: Multi-source bidding is common for larger accounts; switching costs vary (cylinder fleets, tank installations, purity qualifications, safety protocols). Vertical links to production (air separation units, CO₂ sources) can matter for foreclosure theories but are secondary here unless the PE platform or target is meaningfully integrated upstream.

Agencies (FTC and DOJ) have historically reviewed industrial gas and distribution combinations with attention to local depot-level competition, national account effects, and whether “distribution” is a distinct relevant market from production.

================================================================================
III. APPLICABLE LEGAL FRAMEWORK
================================================================================

A. Clayton Act § 7

Section 7 prohibits acquisitions the effect of which “may be substantially to lessen competition, or to tend to create a monopoly” in any line of commerce in any section of the country. Horizontal mergers are evaluated under the DOJ/FTC Merger Guidelines (2023), focusing on:

- Market definition (Brown Shoe factors; hypothetical monopolist / SSNIP where useful)
- Concentration and deltas (HHI frameworks remain informative though not rigid screens)
- Unilateral effects (loss of head-to-head competition, diversion, closeness of substitutes)
- Coordinated effects (if the market is vulnerable to coordination)
- Entry, repositioning, and rival expansion
- Cognizable efficiencies (merger-specific, verifiable, not from anticompetitive output reduction)
- Potential competition and entrenchment theories where applicable to PE roll-ups

B. Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act (HSR)

- Notification thresholds: Size-of-transaction and, where applicable, size-of-person tests (adjusted annually). Confirm current dollar thresholds at filing.
- Filing: Separate Notification and Report Forms by acquiring and acquired persons; filing fees tiered by transaction value.
- Waiting period: Generally 30 calendar days (15 for cash tender/bankruptcy in specified cases), extendable by Second Request. Early termination may be requested but is discretionary and has at times been suspended as a matter of policy — confirm current agency practice at filing.
- Gun-jumping: Parties must remain independent until waiting period expiration; information exchanges and integration planning must stay within counsel-supervised clean-team protocols.
- 4(c)/4(d) documents: Competitive analyses, board books, and banker books discussing markets, shares, customers, and competition must be submitted; document preservation and collection discipline is critical.

C. Other Potential Regimes

- State attorneys general may open parallel reviews, especially if local hospital, municipal, or essential-industry customers are affected.
- Foreign filing: If the target or buyer has sufficient turnover/assets in other jurisdictions, assess EU, UK, Canada, Mexico, Brazil, and other multi-jurisdictional triggers. Industrial gas footprints often create multi-country filing maps even for “U.S. distribution” deals.
- CFIUS / sectoral: Unlikely as a primary path for pure domestic distribution, but flag if foreign PE or sensitive end-markets (defense, semiconductors, medical) are in scope.

================================================================================
IV. ANTITRUST RISK ASSESSMENT
================================================================================

A. Theory of Harm — Horizontal Overlap

The core theory is unilateral effects from combining two distributors that customers view as close substitutes in local or regional markets for specified gas products and delivery modes. Coordinated effects may be secondary where few rivals remain post-deal and pricing is transparent (e.g., published schedule prices plus contract discounts).

Key factual drivers of risk:

1. Product market granularity
   - Packaged industrial gases vs. bulk liquid vs. specialty/medical may be separate markets.
   - Medical oxygen and certain USP/NF gases can draw heightened attention due to healthcare customer effects.
   - Equipment rental and services may be clustered with gas supply or analyzed as aftermarkets.

2. Geographic market definition
   - Depot radius / drive-time analysis for cylinder routes and bulk drops.
   - Overlap maps by branch, fill plant, and customer ship-to locations.
   - National accounts may support a broader geography for a subset of volume.

3. Shares and concentration
   - Party shares by revenue and by volume (scf, tons, cylinders) in each candidate market.
   - HHI and ΔHHI; number of significant remaining rivals (Air Liquide, Linde, Air Products, regional independents, and other PE-backed platforms, as applicable).
   - Win/loss and diversion evidence from CRM, bid files, and sales narratives in 4(c) documents.

4. PE roll-up / serial acquisition context
   - Agencies increasingly scrutinize PE add-on strategies that incrementally raise concentration below prior deal thresholds.
   - Prior acquisitions by the same fund or platform in industrial gases should be inventoried; cumulative effects and ordinary-course documents discussing “platform density” or “pricing power” elevate risk and 4(c) sensitivity.

5. Customer impacts
   - Hospital GPOs, food processors, and sole-source remote sites may claim limited alternatives.
   - Multi-year contracts, tank ownership, and qualification barriers affect ease of switching.

B. Preliminary Risk Rating

| Factor                              | Indicative Direction        | Notes                                      |
|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Horizontal product overlap          | Risk-elevating              | Core issue per engagement framing          |
| Local geographic overlap            | Risk-elevating if dense     | Map depots and routes ASAP                 |
| PE platform / prior add-ons         | Risk-elevating              | Roll-up narrative; document risk           |
| National multi-source competition   | Mitigating if robust        | Big-3 + independents residual competition  |
| Entry / expansion                   | Mixed                       | Depot entry possible but not always timely |
| Efficiencies                        | Mitigating if documented    | Route density, fill optimization, SG&A     |
| Vertical integration                | Case-specific               | Flag if production assets involved         |

Overall preliminary rating: MODERATE — manageable with disciplined filing advocacy and, if needed, targeted local remedies; could rise to MODERATE-HIGH if overlap HHIs are high in multiple MSAs or if medical gas concentration is significant.

C. Open Diligence Items (Priority)

1. Overlap matrix: products × geographies × revenue/volume × customer count.
2. Branch/depot list and radius competitive sets for buyer platform and target.
3. Top-50 customer overlap and dual-source status.
4. Three-year win/loss vs. each other and vs. major rivals.
5. All prior HSR filings and Second Requests involving the PE sponsor’s gas platform.
6. Ordinary-course board decks, IC memos, CIM, and management presentations (4(c)/4(d) harvest).
7. Any non-competes, exclusive supply, or fill agreements that constrain rivals.
8. State licensing (medical gas, compressed gas) and any CON-like constraints.

================================================================================
V. HSR FILING STRATEGY
================================================================================

A. Reportability and Timing

1. Confirm thresholds using current FTC threshold table; include contingent consideration, earn-outs, and assumed liabilities per HSR valuation rules.
2. Identify “acquiring person” and “acquired person” (PE fund structure, GP/LP control, and association rules under the HSR Act and rules — especially for fund families and co-investors).
3. Build a filing calendar working backward from signing and drop-dead dates:
   - Document collection & privilege review: start immediately
   - Draft Item 4 narratives and revenue breakouts: parallel track
   - Pre-filing counsel meet-and-confer on difficult item responses
   - File promptly after signing (or as covenanted); avoid unnecessary delay that compresses remedy time before outside date

B. Filing Posture

1. Request early termination if available under then-current agency practice; do not rely on it for deal timing.
2. Prepare a voluntary white paper or advocacy deck for use if the transaction is pulled for deeper review (PNO inquiry or full investigation), addressing:
   - Proper market definition (local competition remains vigorous)
   - Diversion and closeness (parties not uniquely close)
   - Entry/expansion and customer countervailing power
   - Efficiencies and customer benefits (reliability, safety, capacity)
3. Second Request readiness: data room index for custodian emails, pricing data, customer-level shipments, bid files, and depot economics; identify a response vendor and timeline (often 60–120+ days to substantial compliance if not prepared).

C. Agency Assignment Expectations

Industrial gas matters have historically been reviewed by either FTC or DOJ depending on incumbency and related matters. Clearance strategy should be agency-agnostic in drafting but tailored once clearance responsibility is known. Expect questions on:

- Local share worksheets
- Customer affidavits or complaint risk
- PE hold periods and incentives
- Interlocks / interlocking directorates (Clayton § 8) across portfolio companies

D. Gun-Jumping and Information Exchange

- Implement a clean team for competitively sensitive information (CSI): current pricing, customer-level margins, strategic plans, unannounced bids.
- Integration planning limited to non-CSI workstreams pre-close; no joint customer negotiations or price coordination.
- Train commercial teams; document protocols.

E. Multistate and Foreign Coordination

- Map foreign mandatory filings; sequence U.S. and non-U.S. filings to avoid inconsistent messaging.
- Prepare for state AG information requests if healthcare or public customers are material.

================================================================================
VI. PURCHASE AGREEMENT — ANTITRUST PROVISIONS TO ALIGN WITH STRATEGY
================================================================================

Counsel has flagged markup deviations from firm precedent. The following positions should be aligned with the risk rating:

A. Efforts Standard
- Prefer “reasonable best efforts” or “hell-or-nothing” only if reverse termination fee (RTF) and outside date adequately compensate risk.
- Explicitly address litigation cooperation and appeal obligations if a challenge is filed.

B. Remedy Covenant
- Buyer should retain control over remedy decisions, with a clear cap: e.g., divestitures limited to specified overlap branches / revenue bands; no obligation to divest material non-overlap assets or accept conduct remedies that impair the platform.
- Target cooperation: hold-separate, transitional services, and employee retention for divestiture packages.

C. Timing
- Outside date with automatic extension if only antitrust clearance is outstanding and Second Request is pending, balanced against RTF and ticking fee.
- Filing deadline covenant (e.g., file within 5–10 business days of signing).

D. Termination and Fees
- Antitrust-specific RTF sized to deal value and risk (higher if MODERATE-HIGH after overlap screen).
- Reverse break fee vs. ticking fee tradeoffs; avoid target walk-rights that strand the buyer mid-Second Request without compensation mechanics.

E. Representations
- Antitrust compliance, no pending investigations, accuracy of share estimates used in disclosure schedules — coordinate with diligence findings.

================================================================================
VII. REMEDY PLAYBOOK (CONTINGENT)
================================================================================

If agencies identify problem markets:

1. Structural (preferred): divest discrete depots, cylinder routes, or local business units sufficient to restore competition; identify upfront “fix-it-first” or “upfront buyer” candidates among regional independents or non-overlapping strategics.
2. Scope discipline: avoid national share give-ups where only local issues exist.
3. Behavioral remedies: generally disfavored as standalone fixes for horizontal distribution overlaps; use only as supplements (e.g., short-term supply to divestiture buyer).
4. Timeline: begin confidential banker/process work on contingent divestitures early enough to meet a negotiated outside date.

================================================================================
VIII. RECOMMENDED NEAR-TERM WORKPLAN
================================================================================

Week 0–1
- Stand up antitrust workstream; issue hold notice for 4(c)/4(d).
- Complete overlap heat map and provisional HHI model.
- Confirm HSR reportability, parties, and fee tier.

Week 1–3
- Harvest and privilege-review Item 4 documents.
- Draft HSR forms and internal advocacy memo.
- Align purchase agreement antitrust markup with remedy caps and RTF.
- Install clean-team protocol.

Week 3–Filing
- Finalize forms; mock agency Q&A.
- File HSR; submit voluntary materials only if strategically indicated.
- Activate Second Request vendor on standby.

Post-Filing
- Respond to PNO questions within aggressive SLAs.
- If Second Request: substantial compliance plan, rolling productions, and economic white papers.
- Parallel state/foreign clearances.

================================================================================
IX. CONCLUSIONS AND ADVICE
================================================================================

1. The industrial gas distribution acquisition presents a classic horizontal overlap profile in a PE add-on setting. Substantive risk is real but typically local and remediable if concentration problems are confined.

2. Treat HSR process risk (timing, Second Request burden, gun-jumping) as equal in importance to substantive § 7 risk for deal certainty.

3. Do not sign without: (a) a completed overlap screen informing remedy caps; (b) agreement mechanics that match the risk (efforts, RTF, outside date); and (c) a document collection plan that will withstand Item 4 scrutiny.

4. Next decision gate: present quantitative overlap results and a go/no-go on voluntary agency engagement versus standard filing advocacy.

================================================================================
X. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITATIONS
================================================================================

This memorandum is based on the matter file engagement materials describing an industrial gas distribution PE acquisition with horizontal overlap, including the operative agreement framework (representations, covenants, closing conditions, indemnification, termination) and flagged markup open issues. It does not replace a full market study, customer interviews, or econometric diversion analysis. Thresholds, fee tiers, and early-termination practice should be confirmed against current FTC/DOJ publications at the time of filing. This document is attorney work product prepared for the simulated litigation/corporate law-firm engagement and is not a formal legal opinion for third-party reliance.

END OF MEMORANDUM

- PE hold periods and incentives
- Interlocks / interlocking directorates (Clayton Act Section 8) across portfolio companies

D. Gun-Jumping and Information Exchange

- Implement a clean team for competitively sensitive information (CSI): current pricing, customer-level margins, strategic plans, unannounced bids.
- Integration planning limited to non-CSI workstreams pre-close; no joint customer negotiations or price coordination.
- Train commercial teams; document protocols.

E. Multistate and Foreign Coordination

- Map foreign mandatory filings; sequence U.S. and non-U.S. filings to avoid inconsistent messaging.
- Prepare for state AG information requests if healthcare or public customers are material.

================================================================================
VI. PURCHASE AGREEMENT — ANTITRUST PROVISIONS TO ALIGN WITH STRATEGY
================================================================================

Counsel has flagged markup deviations from firm precedent. The following positions should be aligned with the risk rating:

A. Efforts Standard
- Prefer reasonable best efforts or hell-or-nothing only if reverse termination fee (RTF) and outside date adequately compensate risk.
- Explicitly address litigation cooperation and appeal obligations if a challenge is filed.

B. Remedy Covenant
- Buyer should retain control over remedy decisions, with a clear cap: e.g., divestitures limited to specified overlap branches / revenue bands; no obligation to divest material non-overlap assets or accept conduct remedies that impair the platform.
- Target cooperation: hold-separate, transitional services, and employee retention for divestiture packages.

C. Timing
- Outside date with automatic extension if only antitrust clearance is outstanding and Second Request is pending, balanced against RTF and ticking fee.
- Filing deadline covenant (e.g., file within 5–10 business days of signing).

D. Termination and Fees
- Antitrust-specific RTF sized to deal value and risk (higher if MODERATE-HIGH after overlap screen).
- Reverse break fee vs. ticking fee tradeoffs; avoid target walk-rights that strand the buyer mid-Second Request without compensation mechanics.

E. Representations
- Antitrust compliance, no pending investigations, accuracy of share estimates used in disclosure schedules — coordinate with diligence findings.

================================================================================
VII. REMEDY PLAYBOOK (CONTINGENT)
================================================================================

If agencies identify problem markets:

1. Structural (preferred): divest discrete depots, cylinder routes, or local business units sufficient to restore competition; identify upfront fix-it-first or upfront buyer candidates among regional independents or non-overlapping strategics.
2. Scope discipline: avoid national share give-ups where only local issues exist.
3. Behavioral remedies: generally disfavored as standalone fixes for horizontal distribution overlaps; use only as supplements (e.g., short-term supply to divestiture buyer).
4. Timeline: begin confidential banker/process work on contingent divestitures early enough to meet a negotiated outside date.

================================================================================
VIII. RECOMMENDED NEAR-TERM WORKPLAN
================================================================================

Week 0–1
- Stand up antitrust workstream; issue hold notice for 4(c)/4(d).
- Complete overlap heat map and provisional HHI model.
- Confirm HSR reportability, parties, and fee tier.

Week 1–3
- Harvest and privilege-review Item 4 documents.
- Draft HSR forms and internal advocacy memo.
- Align purchase agreement antitrust markup with remedy caps and RTF.
- Install clean-team protocol.

Week 3–Filing
- Finalize forms; mock agency Q&A.
- File HSR; submit voluntary materials only if strategically indicated.
- Activate Second Request vendor on standby.

Post-Filing
- Respond to PNO questions within aggressive SLAs.
- If Second Request: substantial compliance plan, rolling productions, and economic white papers.
- Parallel state/foreign clearances.

================================================================================
IX. CONCLUSIONS AND ADVICE
================================================================================

1. The industrial gas distribution acquisition presents a classic horizontal overlap profile in a PE add-on setting. Substantive risk is real but typically local and remediable if concentration problems are confined.

2. Treat HSR process risk (timing, Second Request burden, gun-jumping) as equal in importance to substantive Section 7 risk for deal certainty.

3. Do not sign without: (a) a completed overlap screen informing remedy caps; (b) agreement mechanics that match the risk (efforts, RTF, outside date); and (c) a document collection plan that will withstand Item 4 scrutiny.

4. Next decision gate: present quantitative overlap results and a go/no-go on voluntary agency engagement versus standard filing advocacy.

================================================================================
X. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITATIONS
================================================================================

This memorandum is based on the matter file engagement materials describing an industrial gas distribution PE acquisition with horizontal overlap, including the operative agreement framework (representations, covenants, closing conditions, indemnification, termination) and flagged markup open issues. It does not replace a full market study, customer interviews, or econometric diversion analysis. Thresholds, fee tiers, and early-termination practice should be confirmed against current FTC/DOJ publications at the time of filing. This document is attorney work product prepared for the simulated litigation/corporate law-firm engagement and is not a formal legal opinion for third-party reliance.

END OF MEMORANDUM
